etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御(お) (o-, polite prefix) + 祝(いわ)い (iwai, “celebration, a gift or present”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御 (o-, honorific prefix) +‎ 酒 (sake, “alcoholic beverage, (especially) wine”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御 (o-, “honorific prefix”) +‎ 風呂 (furo, “bath”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 叮嚀 (MC teng neng).
Originally meant a musical instrument used in the ancient Chinese military to signal vigilance or caution.(Can this(+) etymology be sourced?)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Shift from previous 三(み)つ (mitsu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
By surface analysis, 三 (mi, “three”) +‎ つ (tsu, generic counter word).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
The most likely derivation is from 二 (futa, “2, two”) +‎ 人 (-ri, counter for persons).
Alternatively, from 二 (fu, “2, two”, short-form) +‎ 人 (-tari, counter for persons).
Yet another probable derivation would be a shift from 二 (futa, “2, two”) +‎ 人 (-tari):
/puta tari/ → */put̚tari/ → /putari/ → /futari/
(Can this(+) etymology be sourced?)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of Middle Chinese elements 二 (ni, “2, two”) +‎ 人 (nin, “man, person”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
⟨pi1to2⟩ → */pʲitə/ → /fito/ → /hito/ → /çito/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pitə.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text: From Early Middle Chinese 人 (MC nyin). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing. Compare Shanghainese nyin.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Late Middle Chinese 人 (MC nyin). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. Compare Mandarin 人 (rén).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. The protoform may have been -tari, see 三人 (mitari, literally “three people”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: (This term, 人, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *n-anu-.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 千 (MC tshen).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text:
⟨ti⟩ → /t͡ɕi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *ti.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 夏(なつ) (natsu, “summer”) + 休(やす)み (yasumi, “vacation; holiday”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 大(だい) (dai-, “very; much”) + 好(す)き (suki, “liking”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pansimay (“to begin”, transitive).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 始む entry.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, though at the time it was exclusively plural. From 子 (ko, “child”) +‎ 共 (-domo, plural suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested as sabusi in the Man'yōshū, completed sometime around 759 CE.
Generally thought to derive from 荒ぶ (sabu, “to be desolate, to be lonely”), modern 錆びる (sabiru, “to rust, to get old”, intransitive).
In early modern times, some dialects shift in reading from /-b-/ to /-m-/, thus creating samishii; similar to 頭 (tsuburi, tsumuri, “head”), in which tsuburi changes to tsumuri, and 煙 (keburi, kemuri, “smoke”), in which keburi changes to kemuri.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kari narazu/ → /karunarazu/ → /kanːarazu/ → /kanarazu/
Shift from 仮(かり)ならず (kari narazu), itself from 仮(かり) (kari, “temporary”) + ならず (narazu), in which the second element is the negative form of either the Classical Japanese copula なり (nari) or the verb なる (naru, “to become”). Therefore, the literal meaning is “not temporary” or “not becoming temporary”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Considered as related to 愛(お)しむ (oshimu), but is morphologically problematic. (Can this(+) etymology be sourced? Particularly: “why is this problematic?; seems plausible related to おっしゃる (osshiaru) with synonymous meaning”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712. Reconstructed as ultimately from Proto-Japonic *paya.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. The muka portion derives from the 未然形 (mizenkei, “incomplete form”) of verb 向く (muku, “to face opposite to something”), implying “that which stands opposite from the present”. The shi portion is suffix し (shi) indicating direction, also found in words 縦し (tatashi, “the standing or vertical direction”), 横し (yokoshi, “the sideways or horizontal direction”). This appears to be a somewhat rare alternative form, more commonly encountered as さ (sa), and may be cognate with the nominalizing adjective ending さ (sa).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 昔, is an alternative spelling (rare) of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
⟨pi1ru⟩ → */pʲiru/ → /ɸiru/ → /hiru/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *piru (“daytime”).
Derived from 日(ひ) (hi, “day”), suffixed with an element ru of unclear meaning. Compare 夜(よる) (yoru, “night, evening”), which seems to use this same ru element.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/tiu/ → /t͡ɕiu/ → /t͡ɕuː/
From Middle Chinese 晝 (MC trjuwH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/pa/ > /ɸa/ > /ha/.
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pa. Cognate with Okinawan 歯 (hā).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 齒 (MC tsyhiX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: /yopapi/ > /yoɸaɸi/ > /yowawi/ > /yowai/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 無(む) (mu, “lack”) + 理(り) (ri, “reason”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 熱 (netsu, “showing intense feeling”) + 心 (shin, “heart”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Modern form of Old Japanese adjective しろし (shiroshi).
⟨siro1si⟩ (classical 終止形 (shūshikei) or terminal form) → ⟨siro1ki1⟩ (classical 連体形 (rentaikei) or attributive form) → /siroi/ (modern shūshikei and rentaikei)
An intervocalic sound-change caused the medial plosive /-k-/ to undergo voicing, then spirantization, then gliding, then being dropped, before /-i, -u, -e, -o/ (Hamano, 2000).
⟨siro1ki1⟩ → */sirʷokʲi/ → */sirʷogʲi/ → */sirʷoɣi/ → */sirʷoji/ → /siroi/ → [ɕiɾo̞i].

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
⟨isi⟩ → /iɕi/
From Old Japanese. First cited in the Man'yōshū of 759. In turn, the Old Japanese is reconstructed as from Proto-Japonic *isoi.
Likely cognate with 磯(いそ) (iso, “pebble; gravel; rocky beach”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 斛 (MC huwk).
The 石 spelling came about through customary use in Japan of this character for the unit of measure.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 石 (MC dzyek).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *tatu.
Doublet of 建(た)つ (tatsu), 勃(た)つ (tatsu, “to have an erection”), 発(た)つ (tatsu, “to depart”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 立つ (tatu, “to stand”), made explicitly into a transitive verb by applying the 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”). Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tatu.
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE in its 未然形 (mizenkei, “irrealis form”), spelled in phonetic man'yōgana as 岐加受 (kikazu). Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kiku.
Cognates
In the Ryukyuan branch of Japonic, cognate with Kikai 聞きゅい (kikyui), Kunigami 聞ちゅん (hichun, shichun), Miyako 聞きぃ (ksïksï), Northern Amami Ōshima 聞きゅり (kikyuri), Okinawan 聞ちゅん (chichun), Okinoerabu 聞きゅん (kikyun), Southern Amami Ōshima 聞きゅむっ (xikyum), Tokunoshima 聞き (kiki), Yaeyama 聞くん (sïkun), Yonaguni 聞ん (kkun), and Yoron 聞きゅん (kikyun).
False cognate of Malayalam കേൾക്കുക (kēḷkkuka).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *waka.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 誰(だれ) (dare, “who”) + か (ka, indefinite particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 運転(うんてん) (unten) + 手(しゅ) (-shu)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Proto-Japonic *pana. The sense as a pronoun is from pointing to one's nose to refer to oneself.
